(CNN) -- Children from a polygamist sect who one mother says are "hurting very badly" in state custody are likely to be returned to their parents, a CNN legal analyst says. FLDS member Margaret Jessop says her children "feel betrayed by adults." A Texas appeals court ruled Thursday that the state had no right to remove hundreds of children from the Fundamentalist Church of Latter-Day Saints' ranch in Eldorado on April 3, based on the suspicion that a few were being sexually abused. A sect mother who has four children in state custody said the matter has not been fully resolved because an appeal to the Texas Supreme Court is possible. "I'm very grateful, but I'd like to see the children in my arms before I rejoice greatly," Margaret Jessop said on CNN's "Larry King Live."  Watch Jessop react to the ruling » . But a permanent reunion of families is likely, said Jeffrey Toobin, CNN senior legal analyst. "Based on this ruling I think it's clear that if it stands, all these kids are going back with their mothers," Toobin said on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360°." Jessop and other FLDS parents said they had been permitted visits with their children in foster care. Zavenda Young said two of her children were sent to Waco, Texas, and two to Hockley, 148 miles away. "They're in Boys and Girls Country in Hockley. And it's just a -- it's an institution," she told host Larry King. Their father, Edson Jessop, said the experience has been rough on the children. "You can see it's a lot of stress on them," he said. "Every time we leave, they go through that trauma again. It's enough to rip your heart out." "They feel betrayed by adults, and they're hurting very badly," Margaret Jessop added. The Texas Child Protective Services Department's Web site says the agency has been "coordinating with many professional service and government agencies to ensure the safety, health and comfort of the children and women in Eldorado." A statement from the agency Thursday said it's working out a response to the court ruling. "Child Protective Services has one duty -- to protect children," the statement said. "When we see evidence that children have been sexually abused and remain at risk of further abuse, we will act. ... We will work with the office of the attorney general to determine the state's next step in this case."

# Texas Appeals Court Rules on FLDS Custody Case, Orders Review of Child Removals

**SAN ANGELO, Texas** — A Texas appeals court issued a ruling this week addressing the custody status of children removed from the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS) compound, in a decision that could reshape how child welfare officials handle mass removals in future cases involving religious communities.

The Third Court of Appeals found that state child welfare officials had not provided sufficient individualized evidence to justify removing many of the children from their parents, though the court stopped short of ordering immediate reunification for all families. The ruling instructed lower courts to reassess custody arrangements on a case-by-case basis rather than treating the sect as a single household.

"The Department of Family and Protective Services must demonstrate that each child was at risk of abuse or neglect — not rely solely on the fact that they were raised within this particular community," the court wrote in its opinion.

## Parents React with Cautious Relief

For families connected to the sect's Yearning For Zion Ranch, the ruling brought a mixture of relief and lingering anxiety.

"We have been saying since day one that they took our children without any real evidence against us individually," said Merrianne Jessop, a mother whose children were among those removed. "This ruling doesn't fix everything, but it says what we've known — that you can't punish every family for what a few might have done."

Another parent, who asked to be identified only by her first name, Rebecca, out of concern for her family's privacy, expressed frustration at the length of the legal process.

"My children have been gone for months. Every day matters when you're a mother separated from her child," she said. "I'm glad the court is finally looking at us as individuals and not just as part of some group they've already judged."

Not all parents expressed full confidence in the outcome. Some worried the ruling's emphasis on case-by-case review could prolong proceedings rather than resolve them quickly.

## Legal Analysts Weigh In

Legal observers say the ruling underscores a recurring tension in child welfare law: balancing the state's duty to protect children with parents' constitutional rights, particularly when a religious community's practices are viewed with suspicion by outsiders.

"This decision is significant because it reaffirms a basic principle — that removal of a child from parental custody requires specific evidence related to that child, not guilt by association," said Diane Holloway, a family law professor and legal analyst. "Texas child welfare officials faced enormous pressure to act quickly given allegations of underage marriage and abuse within the sect, but the appellate court is signaling that due process protections don't disappear because a case involves an unconventional or controversial community."

Holloway noted that the ruling does not exonerate the FLDS community or dismiss the state's underlying concerns about certain practices, including allegations that some underage girls had been married to older men.

"The court isn't saying abuse didn't happen," she said. "It's saying the state's approach — removing more than 400 children in one sweep — went further than the evidence supported for many of these families. Going forward, caseworkers will likely need to build individualized case files that can withstand this kind of scrutiny."

## Case Sent Back for Further Proceedings

The ruling sends many of the custody cases back to trial courts, where judges will be required to conduct individualized hearings to determine whether specific children should remain in state custody, be returned to their parents, or be placed under supervised arrangements.

Officials with the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services said they were reviewing the ruling's implications and had not yet determined how many cases would be immediately affected.

"Our priority remains and has always been the safety of children," a department spokesperson said in a statement. "We will comply with the court's instructions while continuing to pursue our mission to protect those who cannot protect themselves."

Attorneys representing several of the families said they expect the case to continue working through the courts for months, with some custody determinations likely to be appealed further depending on the outcome of the individualized hearings.

The case has drawn national attention since the initial raid on the YFZ Ranch, prompting broader debate over religious liberty, child protection standards, and the limits of state intervention in matters of family and faith.

*This story will be updated as developments occur.*

**AUSTIN, Texas** — The long-running legal dispute over the custody of children removed from the Yearning For Zion Ranch could be headed to the Texas Supreme Court, as attorneys representing the polygamous sect and state child welfare officials remain at odds over the fate of hundreds of minors taken into state custody.

The case, which has drawn national attention since the initial raid on the ranch belonging to the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, has moved through lower appellate courts with mixed results, setting the stage for a potential showdown before the state's highest civil court.

## Legal Analysts Weigh In

CNN senior legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin, commenting on the proceedings, noted the unusual complexity of the case given its scale and the constitutional questions at stake.

"This is really unprecedented in terms of the sheer number of children involved," Toobin said. "You have serious Fourth Amendment concerns about the initial search and seizure, First Amendment questions about religious practice, and then you have the state's legitimate interest in protecting children from potential abuse. The Texas Supreme Court, if they take this up, is going to have to balance all of these competing interests in a case that doesn't have a lot of direct precedent."

Toobin added that the outcome could have ramifications beyond this specific case. "However this shakes out, it's going to inform how child welfare agencies approach these mass-removal situations in the future, particularly involving closed religious communities."

## CPS Defends Its Actions

Officials with Texas Child Protective Services have maintained that their intervention was necessary and lawful, based on evidence gathered during the initial investigation.

A spokesperson for the Department of Family and Protective Services, which oversees CPS, issued a statement defending the agency's conduct throughout the case:

"Our sole priority from day one has been the safety and well-being of these children. The evidence our investigators gathered gave us reasonable cause for concern about a pattern of abuse within this community. We stand by the professionalism and diligence of our caseworkers, who were operating under extraordinarily difficult circumstances involving a large number of children and limited cooperation from some family members."

The spokesperson added that the agency would respect whatever direction the courts provide moving forward. "We will comply fully with any rulings issued by Texas courts, including the Supreme Court should they choose to hear this matter. Our goal remains ensuring these children are safe, whether that means returning them to their families under appropriate safeguards or pursuing other protective measures."

## What Comes Next

Should the Texas Supreme Court agree to hear the case, legal observers expect arguments to center on whether the initial removal of children was justified under Texas law, and whether subsequent court proceedings adequately protected the due process rights of the affected families.

No timeline has been set for whether the high court will grant review. Attorneys on both sides say they are prepared to continue litigating the matter as long as necessary.
